title: Which soul is God’s work?
source_text: Ἔτι δὲ καὶ τοῦτό φαμεν τῷ Κέλσῳ εἰπόντι· ψυχὴ μὲν θεοῦ ἔργον, σώματος δὲ ἄλλη φύσις καὶ οὐ μόνον ἀκατασκευάστως τὸ τηλικοῦτον δόγμα ῥίψαντι ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀδιορίστως· οὐ γὰρ ἐσαφήνισε, πότερον πᾶσα ψυχὴ θεοῦ ἔργον ἢ μόνη ἡ λογική· φαμὲν τοίνυν πρὸς αὐτόν· εἰ μὲν πᾶσα ψυχὴ θεοῦ ἔργον, δηλονότι καὶ τῶν ἀλόγων καὶ εὐτελεστάτων, ἵνα καὶ παντὸς σώματος ἄλλη φύσις ᾖ παρὰ τὴν τῆς ψυχῆς. ἔοικε μέντοι ἐν τοῖς ἑξῆς. ἐν οἷς καὶ θεοφιλέστερα τὰ ἄλογα ζῷά φησιν ἡμῶν καὶ τοῦ θείου τὴν ἔννοιαν ἔχειν καθαρωτέραν, παριστάνειν ὅτι οὐ μόνον ἡ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἀλλὰ πολὺ μᾶλλον καὶ ἡ τῶν ἀλόγων ζῴων ψυχὴ ἔργον ἐστὶ τοῦ θεοῦ· τοῦτο γὰρ ἀκολουθεῖ τῷ θεοφιλέστερα λέγεσθαι ἐκεῖνα ἡμῶν. εἰ δὲ μόνη ἡ λογικὴ ψυχὴ θεοῦ ἔργον ἐστὶ, πρῶτον μὲν οὐκ ἐσαφήνισε τὸ τοιοῦτον· δεύτερον δὲ ἀκολουθεῖ τῷ ἀδιορίστως εἰρῆσθαι περὶ τῆς ψυχῆς, ὡς οὐ πάσης ἀλλὰ μόνης τῆς λογικῆς οὔσης θεοῦ ἔργον. τὸ μηδὲ παντὸς σώματος (ἄλλην) εἶναι φύσιν. εἰ δὲ μὴ παντὸς σώματος ἄλλη φύσις, ἀλλ᾿ ἑκάστου ἐστὶ τὸ σῶμα ζῴου ἀνάλογον τῇ ψυχῇ, δῆλον ὅτι οὗ ψυχὴ θεοῦ ἔργον ἐστὶ, διαφέροι ἂν τὸ ταύτης σῶμα σώματος, ἐν ᾧ οἰκεῖ ψυχὴ οὐκ οὖσα ἔργον θεοῦ. καὶ οὕτω ψεῦδος ἔσται τὸ μηδὲν διοίσειν νυκτερίδος ἢ εὐλῆς ἢ βατράχου σῶμα παρὰ τὸ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου.
pass_a_gloss: Further we say this also to Celsus, who said: soul is God's work, but of body another nature, and who threw out (ῥίπτω) so great a doctrine not only without proof (ἀκατασκευάστως) but also without distinction (ἀδιορίστως); for he did not make clear (σαφηνίζω) whether every soul is God's work or only the rational (λογική). We say therefore to him: if every soul is God's work, plainly also those of the irrational (ἄλογος) and most worthless (εὐτελής superl.), so that (ἵνα) of every body also there is another nature beside (παρά) that of the soul. He seems (ἔοικε), however, in what follows, in which he says that irrational animals are more God-loved (θεοφιλής comp.) than we and have a purer (καθαρός comp.) notion (ἔννοια) of the divine (τὸ θεῖον), to present (παριστάνω) that not only the soul of men but much more that of irrational animals is God's work; for this follows from those being called more God-loved than we. But if only the rational soul is God's work, first, he did not make such clear; second, it follows from its having been said without distinction about the soul, as of not every but only the rational being God's work, that not of every body is there another nature. But if not of every body another nature, but the body of each animal (ζῷον) is analogous (ἀνάλογος) to the soul, plainly the body of that whose soul is God's work would differ from a body in which dwells (οἰκέω) a soul not being God's work. And so it will be false (ψεῦδος) that the body of bat or worm or frog will differ in nothing from that of man.
pass_b_english: We say this further to Celsus, who said, “The soul is the work of God, but the body is of another nature,” and who tossed out so great a doctrine not only without proof but also without drawing distinctions; for he did not make clear whether every soul is God’s work or only the rational soul. So we say to him: if every soul is God’s work, then clearly the souls of irrational and utterly worthless creatures are so too, so that every body as well is of another nature than the soul. And indeed in what follows, where he says that irrational animals are dearer to God than we are and have a purer notion of the divine, he seems to represent not only the soul of men but much more the soul of irrational animals as God’s work; for this follows from saying that they are dearer to God than we are.

But if only the rational soul is God’s work, then, first, he did not make this clear; and second, from his having spoken of the soul without distinction, taken to mean that not every soul but only the rational soul is God’s work, it follows that not every body is of another nature either. And if not every body is of another nature, but the body of each living creature corresponds to its soul, clearly the body of a creature whose soul is God’s work would differ from a body in which there dwells a soul that is not God’s work. And so it will be false that the body of a bat or a maggot or a frog will differ in nothing from that of a man.

choices.choice: Celsus's formula (4.52) aligned with the 4.chunk9 rendering: 'the soul is the work of God, but the body is of another nature', 'maggot' for εὐλή, 'what is perishable in them is alike'
ἄλλη φύσις kept as 'of another nature' throughout so the argument reads straight
ὡς οὐ πάσης …: 'taken to mean that', not 'as though'
'the souls of irrational and utterly worthless creatures'; 'maggot'

Koetschau's supplied ⟨ἄλλην⟩ in τὸ μηδὲ παντὸς σώματος ⟨ἄλλην⟩ εἶναι φύσιν (shown as '(ἄλλην)' in the staged text) is followed. The opening quotation repeats Celsus's words from 4.52 and is put in quotation marks. His claim that irrational animals are dearer to God and have a purer notion of the divine refers to a later passage of Celsus's work (ἐν τοῖς ἑξῆς). Origen gives it here as indirect report, so it is not put in quotation marks. ἵνα … ᾖ is taken as result ('so that'), not purpose. ἀνάλογον τῇ ψυχῇ is rendered 'corresponds to its soul'. No Scripture in this chapter.
